I agree with you on the memory modules.

But, up until now the addressable sector size for storage was 512 bytes (up to 528 on SAS/SCSI).

We're only now (last couple of years) moving over to 4KiB (up to 4.125KiB on SAS) sector size, on par with the RAM memory page size, but we're still in the transition phase through 512e (not yet in 4Kn).

This means that on most installations, sectors are still addressed in 512 byte chucks wich introduce the following problem: If one reads 2 * 512B contiguous sectors over 512e, the drive reads either 1 * 4KiB or 2 * 4KiB sectors in order to fulfill the request. This represents up to 700% overhead in this particular worst-case scenario.

And the drive still has to spend its time emulating/translating 512e addresses into 4Kn addresses.

So better to give the drive less commands for more contiguous sectors, rather than give it more commands for less contiguous sectors. It's as simple as that.
Good point about sector sizes. I'd assume that any modern filesystem would use larger chunks than even that, e.g. 1MB contiguous chunks unless the file is really small.

The default (C:) cluster size on an NTFS drive these days (Win10) is at 4KiB (max is at 1MiB).

Each fragment of a file would be one or multiple 4KiB. Even larger files are split into 4KiB (cluster size) chunks.

On buffered reads/writes the system would read at least one 4KiB contiguous chunk (8*512bytes). These chunks would be aligned with the underlying 4Kn format of the drive so, at this point, the worst-case scenario above is avoided.

Once the application has loaded the file, it may issue commands that were never optimized for 4Kn chunks but only for 512. Some of these may not be buffered, or could not be buffered. This is where the scenario above may apply.

Because in both cases you have to consult the file system to find out which sectors contain your file, and in both cases you have to read the contents of 9 sectors. It's not going to take any longer to read one address over another.

In its most general form, it's the Bin Packing problem, and it's more specifically the Knapsack Problem in this case.

For the Knapsack Problem:

  • The decision problem form of the knapsack problem (...) is NP-complete, thus there is no known algorithm both correct and fast (polynomial-time) in all cases.

  • While the decision problem is NP-complete, the optimization problem is NP-hard, its resolution is at least as difficult as the decision problem, and there is no known polynomial algorithm which can tell, given a solution, whether it is optimal (...).

To have a file which is not fragmented, you need to solve this problem with an optimized solution (no inter-gaps in your file) and you need to do it like yesterday, because with each CPU cycle spent on this problem, the write IOPS drops.

Middle ground: "We'll just do a little fragmentation but fast"
